en: Homage to Tārā!
Those who are devoted to ritual bathing and purification, yet who revile monks and lay devotees.
Now, this reasoning is being stated for the sake of pacifying their delusion. || 1 ||
For even that which is pure indeed arises from feces, urine, and so forth;
therefore, how can this body, composed of impurities, be made stainless? (2)
Even though it is constantly praised and touched again and again, what indeed is there in the body? It is just like a jar filled with excrement.
The five products of the cow are drunk and pure food is eaten;
yet even that, once it has entered within, turns into excrement and reaches the state of urine. (4)
Even the water that is poured into the mouth for the sake of purifying the body becomes impure; what then is the use of performing the ritual rinsing (ācamana)?
If that which has not been touched by substances such as feces or urine is purified by contact with those very same things, what is the use of ritual sipping (ācamana)?
Why do not the leftover shards of pots, once washed with water, attain the state of being established in reality; and why not even dogs and pigs, once bathed with water, become pure? (7)
Excrement, urine, impurities, phlegm, nails, hair, and so forth—all these originate from one's own body; how then can they attain purity? (8)
Impurity flees, the dust is removed, and the stench of heat is destroyed;
this alone is the supreme goal achieved when bathing is performed.
All the water in the entire network of the Ganges' channels and pools is one and the same;
and although the earth has but a single nature, it will not become a sacred ford.
[134] Earth is not the water at a sacred ford, nor is it the pool or the network of channels of the Gaṅgā;
the mind alone is the great sacred ford, where by bathing one becomes pure. (11)
Or if even a small amount of merit cannot be established, because this primary deity would become agitated within oneself. (12)

For one whose intention is crooked, there is no recollection of mantras, no worship, no chanting, no meditation, and no self-restraint; everything for such a person is indeed in disorder due to their distorted application.
To perform the worship of the deity after having eaten is inconsistent with that;
for even the food would be pure only if the body were perfectly clean. (14)
Just as a lump [of charcoal] is the same whether it is not eaten or even when eaten, can a piece of charcoal that is black by nature ever become white even if washed? (15)
Indeed, everything would be edible, for everything is indeed so;
for within food, everything from what is edible to what is inedible, down to excrement, urine, and so forth—whatever substance exists—is medicine. (16)
"By drinking poison one may die, but by [drinking] water one lives"—such is the nature of defects and virtues; the duty of all castes does not remain fixed. || 17 ||
If [the nature of sin belongs to] a Śūdra, then how could it belong to a Brāhmaṇa as well?
For whatever substance is one's own nature, that remains so in every respect.
The world wanders about with its purpose obscured; it does not censure what is fit or unfit to eat.
How can that cow be impure? How can the dog be untouchable? (19)
Having taken hold of the nature of the self, everything is indeed composed of suchness (tathatā).
Just as a heap of sandalwood is composed of suchness, so too is a heap of excrement. // 20 //
If no fault can be found due to the mutual contact of their minds, then a Brahmin who is impure would likewise become a pure dog. (21)
O Brahmins, if a woman were impure, having formed a union with a *ḍomba* man, she would become a *ḍombī*;
[those who] rely upon her would likewise [be so].
Likewise, why should a Śūdra not become [something else] again through contact with a Śūdra woman? || 22 ||
The supreme fault belongs to the highest; for the lowly, it arises from association. But how could a fault arise again through the union of two superior beings? (23)
If there is a fault in reality from the conjunction of both, then why does a single thing become red through its conjunction with turmeric? (24)
The sprout would suffer damage when there is damage to the seed;
however, the earth does not suffer damage through the fault of the seed. (25)
If there were harm to the worlds and to living beings, the connection to life would have come equally to all living beings. (26)
Just as there is no killing of a cow that is either less or more [severe] based on the specific type of cow, so too, its killing does not remain without distinction. (27)
Just as there is no [distinction] superior to water in terms of its range for a particular type of cow, so too it is said that [there is no distinction] superior to a particular living being. 28.
To whatever extent evil has been committed, to that same extent the supreme [merit] has been performed;
for him there shall be no increase, nor does any diminution arise. (29)
Sin does not afflict men; rather, merit is afflicted by sin.
By this [knowledge], one understands that everything consists of the nature of pleasure and pain. (30)
And as for that ground which has become dissolved, whatever speech has been accumulated therein, there is not the slightest stain; only the supreme worldly activity is performed. (31)
All this—sleeping, eating, and sexual intercourse—is natural. How can one do these things even after being adorned, if one is shaven-headed? (32)

In some places cow-flesh is eaten, and in others it is consumed by Śūdras; even a dog [eats] in the food [of some]. Thus, the course of worldly life proceeds according to the distinctions between people. 33.
Only he who performs [the prescribed] actions becomes a Brāhmaṇa; for if a Brāhmaṇa exists merely by virtue of his body, he does not abide in the true nature of his caste.
Alternatively, if caste were something inherent in one's very nature,
then even by eating the food of a Śūdra, one would not fall into the state of a Śūdra. (35)
If the son of a Śūdrī does not observe the vow because he is a Śūdra, would even the son of a Brāhmaṇa become a Brāhmaṇa [merely by that]? (36)

Those born from the seed of a Brāhmaṇa but produced from the womb of a Śūdra woman are not Brāhmaṇas in the first generation, nor are they Śūdras; rather, they become entirely [of an intermediate status]. || 37 ||
A Brahmin devoid of ritual action is inferior even to a Śūdra;
whereas a Śūdra endowed with ritual action is superior even to a Brahmin. (38)
Just as among cows a milch-cow of tawny hue is honored, so too among men is the man endowed with virtues honored. (39)
"This one is a Brahmin, that one is a Śūdra, this one is a Caṇḍāla, and that one is an actor;
in food, this one is a Caṇḍāla—only by name are they different, but their essential nature is not otherwise. (40)
Just as a Śūdrī, a Ḍombī, and a Cāṇḍālī are likewise [regarded as] a virtuous wife (satī), so too is the entire world of existence of a single form; no distinction is seen anywhere. (41)
The entire bhaga is of a single form, and the linga likewise is indeed one;
everything is marked by the limbs of the bhaga and linga, for there is no limb that is without the bhaga.
The horse would not be its own self, nor would the horse be the self of the horse; the pig would not be its own self, nor would the pig [be the self] of the pig.
For all beings there is but one Self; it is pure consciousness alone, while [individuals] are distinct only in their externality.
All embodied beings indeed exist as living beings; for all of them, everything consists of pleasure and pain, and it is exactly so for everyone. (44)
Just as there is a lineage of fish and turtles, and likewise of elephants and boars, so indeed is the lineage of all beings; it is not otherwise. (45)
Substance becomes substance upon obtaining [its cause], and knowledge arises from the application of knowledge;
everything is born from their conjunction, just as a pot is produced from the action of a potter. (46)
If pleasure arises from the practice of yoga through the eating of what is not to be eaten,
then everything arises from conjunction, just as a jar is produced from its constituent parts.
All this is mere illusion; from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is neither self nor other.
Conventional practice is established for the sake of worldly affairs; otherwise, social interaction would be impossible. (48)
Whatever is respected by the world, that alone attains the status of authority;
and there is no inquiry into that, just as a barbarian [accepts] a scholar [as an authority]. 49.
That which was previously non-existent does not function in the world;
nor does there exist in the world a self-acting agent or a self-knowing knower. (50)
Just as that was previously performed there by me, the Origin of the World, so too does a person engage in activity through that darkness. (51)
Just as a variegated figure painted with various colors is seen to be beautiful, why is it that everything else is entirely red? (52)

In all cases, the fault of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is not a fault from the perspective of ultimate reality; for those whose minds are pure, the fault of latent impressions does not abide anywhere. (53)
The world is not serene for him whose awakening is not found;
indeed, for one whose mind is disciplined, everything is entirely serene through awakening. 54.
For one who lacks self-awareness, there can be no awakening; what indeed can a lamp do for a blind person, even if it is aflame? (55)
Where there is no virtuous person, just as there is no core within the trunk of a plantain tree, even the exertion of Fate is in vain; what fruit can there be? 56.
Where one has not personally realized and thereby abandoned the conceptualization of "mind," how could there be true comprehension through the awakening of another? (57)
As long as the self is not even perceived by one's own eyes when going there oneself, so too does it exist [only] through the cognitions of objects, even after hearing the word. 58.
[138] [4A] Who would strive for their own sake in crushing the enemy of anger? For what purpose is dry leather? Affliction is appropriate only where greed is perceived. (59)
Just as a bee, having searched through thousands of millions of flowers, goes to that flower which is a vessel of nectar and enjoys it; (50)
Just as a fisherwoman takes the husk while leaving the grain within,
so too, even toward one who knows reality, he preserves the truth through debate.
If accomplishment were attained by eating what is not to be eaten or by approaching those who should not be approached, then why would accomplishment not also belong to the sow and the bitch? (62)
O noble lady, what are the perfected ones?
Whatever bodily [action] exists, and whatever vocal [action] remains—all evil and all merit are comprised solely within the mind. (63)
Even when being propitiated, that deity does not attain satisfaction so long as he does not perceive the affliction arising from the acquisition of a sentient being. (64)
Even merit does not belong to one for whom no evil exists;
who could be superior to a beast, being entirely free from both evil and merit? (65)
Everything struck down by the power of gnosis does not remain even as a single thing;
action is indeed non-action anywhere, and everywhere there is both action and non-action.
The practitioner in union attains true yoga when his fitness remains;
and the yogi who has conquered that fitness lives beyond the mere name.
Those various faults and those various virtues which are not within the range of everyone—like a lamp situated inside a jar, it may possess qualities yet appear devoid of them. (68)
A substance emits a foul odor when it has decomposed, just as a man with a cleft palate [speaks indistinctly]; thus, the true nature of both form and the self must necessarily be declared. (69)
Whatever object exists wherever it may be, and by whatever means it may exist—even if it is something never before perceived—why do yogins not know all of that? (70)
Just as an eye specially prepared with medicinal herbs can see even in the darkness as if it were daylight, so too [is this case]. (71)
All knowledge arises when the power of jewels and mantras is present;
for the powers of medicinal herbs, jewels, and mantras are indeed immeasurable. (72)
The power of mantras certainly exists, and knowledge certainly exists within living beings;
yet, the result produced by another will not become manifest as long as the mind is not purified. (73)
Fire certainly exists within chaff; why does it not burn at all times?
When there is wind and dry grass, then its subsequent action occurs. (74)
Just as the power of fire is dull when it is weak, so too there exists some substance which, being such, would not manifest itself. 75.
At that time, would there not be the attainment of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs, as well as access to those who are otherwise unapproachable?
And would not those [powers] such as Śūkarī and Kukkurī also be accomplished? (76)
The one whose intention is pure attains everything that belongs to him—[the power of] jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs, and the treasury of the vision of Bhāra. (77)
Whatever the disposition of one may be, such shall be their fruit;
all fruit arises from disposition, and it is rendered fruitless by great accumulations [of material things]. (78)
By whatever means possible, one should lead the mind to purity;
once the mind has been led to purity, everything indeed becomes perfectly pure. 79.
The mind is a god, the mind is a demon; the mind is established as everything.
Yet, due to the absence of mental activity, even that single mind does not remain. (80)
Wherever one should fix the mind, there the supreme state arises;
therein alone one attains perfection—what is the use of a royal net? (81)
The deity resides right here, and the mantra likewise resides right here; everything is accomplished right here—why then this exertion elsewhere? (82)
For one whose faith does not remain even after reflecting upon everything,
the fruit shall arise everywhere for those whose minds are endowed with faith. (83)
He who has reached the ultimate goal everywhere, whose self is established in the final state, is the Lord of Existence;
for him in whom no finality remains, nothing whatsoever is accomplished.
For those whose minds are free from intrinsic nature, without support, and untainted, the activities of Māra will undoubtedly be brought to an end. || 85 ||
All of saṃsāra is unstable, like water droplets on a lotus leaf;
the breath may not remain for even a moment—when will death occur? (86)
Just as the light of a firefly or the nature of water bubbles, so too is all this; nothing possesses permanence.
Just as a dream is perceived with absolute certainty due to unstable cognition, so too is all this; for whom is it not merely a mental construction? (88)
Just as an object seen at one moment is not seen in that same way again, therefore this entire discourse must be momentary and not stable. (89)
That house where the roof-covering is constantly repaired and where the frog is not killed shall endure for a long time. (90)
This nature is the power of space, and knowledge is non-conceptual;
yet even for that which is one, there exists bondage, characterized by cutting and piercing. (91)
The Buddha is the Lord of the All-Knowing, the Lord of the Three Worlds, and the Sovereign;
he is the Great Emptiness of all things, transcending the world, yet [appearing as] the worldly. 92.
As is the Buddha, so is Viṣṇu; as is Viṣṇu, so is Śiva.
Everything is thus for them; no distinction whatsoever has been shown. 93.
Everything—jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth—is accomplished when kept secret;
everything is rendered ineffective when not kept secret, including fasting and the accumulation of merit. (94)
Having weighed all other scriptures, the Vedas, the Vedānta, and the Āgamas against it,
the great vow of the Śūdra is one of salutation with the hands joined in reverence. 95.
Neither ritual action, nor vow, nor pilgrimage site, nor bathing, nor worship of the gods—none of these remain, even a single one, for those endowed with non-dual knowledge. (96)
There is no fault in drinking liquor, nor is there even the slightest fruit [to be gained from it];
the yogi should contemplate that enjoyment by which he may become one who approaches liberation. 97.
Through knowledge one attains liberation; knowledge is attained through merit.
Through food [is attained]...
for the sake of purifying the meritorious mind, knowledge is also self-conviction. 98.
That flower is not seen, nor is its fragrance, nor its taste;
for that knowledge is immeasurable, being self-evident like the nature of space itself. 99.
Because it is the means of valid cognition for another [cognition] in succession, it is apprehended by itself;
thus, among all dharmas, the Guru is the supreme proponent of the doctrine of causality. 100.
Furthermore, all this that has been described, whatever it may be, is seen as a real entity for a single moment, but is not seen again in that same way. (101)
A water-jar carries water only so long as it is not worn out;
when it reaches a state of decay, what water can that jar carry? || 102 ||
What could carry water?
Although the Self resides within the body, in which specific location does it abide?
No one perceives what its beautiful form is or what its shape is. 103.
Who is old, or who is young? What could be pleasant or painful?
How is there birth, and how is there death? Why does no one see anything at all? 104.
Thus ends the Śucikaraṇa composed by Kāṇeripā.
May there be auspiciousness.
